source_read: PMC HTML (PMC4747759; the published PNAS version, 113(5):E500-E508, not an author manuscript), read in full on 2026-10-31: Significance, Abstract, introduction, Methods (including the subsection on marijuana measurement in the MTFS), Results, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion, Acknowledgments, footnotes; Tables 1-5 and Tables S1-S6, which the PMC page prints in the article body, read as text. Fig. 1 (Vocabulary decline) not inspected (browser pane hidden, screenshots blank). The separate SI file was not opened.

claims.overstatement: None in strength: the claim reports the co-twin results as 'did not differ significantly' with wide intervals, not as evidence of no effect, and does not adopt the authors' conclusion that the decline is due to confounding rather than cannabis. One clarity point: 'fell 4.0 and 3.4 points further behind age peers' is a difference in change between those who used and those who did not. On raw means, those who used fell 1.8 and 2.5 points while those who did not rose 1.8 and 1.3.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude checks against Tables 3, 5, S4 and S6: 789 and 2,277; −4.0 (−6.3 to −1.7) and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3); −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5) and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) with binge drinking and other drug use; identical pairs −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5; 25) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4; 112); non-identical −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99); 47 heavy-use pairs −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6). Exposure (ever use on any occasion by follow-up against never), ages (9-12 to 17-20) and adjustment set (age, sex, race, zygosity, SES, MTFS cohort) match. The missing part: 'but not on four other subtests' leaves out the Information subtest. In the MTFS, the only cohort that gave it, those who used declined 2.0 points more (−3.3 to −0.7, P = 0.002), and the authors' main reading rests on Vocabulary and Information together. Six subtests were given in all: Vocabulary declined in both cohorts, Information in the one that gave it, and the other four (Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Arrangement) showed no difference. Information also fell to −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9) after adjustment for drinking and other drugs. Suggested addition: 'and on Information (−2.0, −3.3 to −0.7; MTFS only)'. Smaller points: 'lower scores preceded use' holds for Vocabulary (−1.9), Information (−2.7) and Block Design (−2.0) at 11-12 in the MTFS, but there were no baseline differences in the RFAB. 'Intervals wide enough to include the between-family differences' holds for the identical pairs and the RFAB non-identical pairs; the MTFS non-identical interval (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes −3.4. Among those who used, use more than 30 times or daily use was not linked with more decline (Table 4). Half the later MTFS sample was recruited for disruptive behaviour. Attrition was high in the RFAB: 427 of 1,241 lacked cannabis data and had lower baseline IQ and SES, and 323 of 789 had no follow-up IQ. Table 5 has three P values that do not match their intervals (see the anchor); none changes significance.

anchors.locator: Methods › Participants and Procedure (RFAB, MTFS), 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: RFAB: 614 families, 1,241 twins and triplets from Los Angeles schools, enrolled 2001 at 9-10, assessed at 9-10, 11-13, 14-15, 16-18 and 19-20; 52% female, 46% MZ; Hispanic 37%, Caucasian 27%, mixed 17%, African American 14%, Asian 5%. MTFS: two Minnesota population samples (original younger cohort n = 1,527, 1990-1996; Enrichment Study n = 1,000, 1999-2006, half selected for disruptive behaviour and academic disengagement), recruited at 11, followed about every 3 years; 51% female, 63% MZ, 93% Caucasian; the two samples combined.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Assessment of intelligence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: RFAB: four WASI subtests (Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning) at 9-10 and 19-20. MTFS: four WISC-R subtests (Vocabulary, Information, Block Design, Picture Arrangement) at 11-12 and the same WAIS-R subtests at 17-19; the Enrichment sample had only Vocabulary and Block Design at follow-up. Scores age-standardized and put on an IQ metric (mean 100, SD 15).

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Assessment of marijuana use, 1st paragraph; Measurement of Marijuana Use in the Minnesota Twin Family Study, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ever use = any use on any occasion, self-reported (RFAB survey at each wave; MTFS interviews plus a private computerized survey, taking the highest endorsement). Frequent use = 30 or more times; daily use for 6-12 months by 19-20 (RFAB) or 17-19 (MTFS). No measure of recency; current and former use not separated (Limitations, 4th paragraph).

anchors.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Table S1
anchors.extracted: Analytic samples: RFAB 789 twins (436 families; 475 who used, 314 who did not; 60%), MTFS 2,277 (1,171 families; 822 and 1,455; 36%). Among those who used: more than 30 times 49.3% (RFAB) and 37.0% (MTFS), daily use 20.8% and 22.6%; other drug use 38.3% against 1.6%, and 39.4% against 6.6%. In the MTFS, those who used were more often male and non-Caucasian and had lower SES (48.6 against 52.1 percentile). Excluded for missing cannabis data: 427 (RFAB) and 220 (MTFS).

anchors.locator: Results › Baseline Differences in IQ, 1st paragraph; Table 2
anchors.extracted: RFAB: no baseline differences. MTFS: those who later used scored lower at 11-12 on Vocabulary (−1.9, P < 0.01), Information (−2.7, P < 0.001) and Block Design (−2.0, P < 0.01). Vocabulary means: RFAB users 99.9 to 98.1, others 100.2 to 102.0; MTFS users 98.8 to 96.3, others 100.7 to 102.0.

anchors.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Difference in change, those who used against those who did not (time-by-use interaction), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and MTFS cohort: Vocabulary −4.0 (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7, P = 0.001) RFAB and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3, P < 0.001) MTFS; Information −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7, P = 0.002), MTFS only. No difference: Similarities −0.1 and Matrix Reasoning 1.9 (RFAB), Block Design 0.2 and −0.6, Picture Arrangement 0.4 (MTFS).
Information subtest: −2.0 points (−3.3 to −0.7), P = 0.002 in the MTFS. The claim's 'but not on four other subtests' omits this significant decline on a fifth subtest.

anchors.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st paragraph (last sentence); Table S4
anchors.extracted: Adding maximal binge drinking and other drug use: Vocabulary −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5, P = 0.022) RFAB and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6, P = 0.244) MTFS; Information −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9, P = 0.399); described as substantially attenuated and no longer significant in the MTFS.

anchors.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 3rd paragraph; Table 4; Table S5
anchors.extracted: Among those who used, use more than 30 times or daily use was not associated with more decline on any subtest (e.g., Vocabulary daily use −0.4, −4.5 to 3.7, RFAB; −0.7, −2.7 to 1.4, MTFS), also after adjustment for other substances. The authors note that the measures do not allow a full dose-response test.

anchors.locator: Results › Comparison of Effect Size Between RFAB and MTFS, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Vocabulary per year of age: RFAB those who did not use 0.01 (P = 0.90), those who used −0.39 (P < 0.001), difference 0.397 per year, about 3.97 points over 10 years; MTFS +0.12 (P = 0.028) and −0.45 (P < 0.001), difference 0.57, about 4.00 points over 7 years; the two studies did not differ (0.176, P = 0.35).

anchors.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 5
anchors.extracted: Twin pairs discordant for ever use, change in the twin who used minus the co-twin: Vocabulary MZ −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, P = 0.098; 25 pairs, RFAB) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, P = 0.639; 112, MTFS); DZ −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99). No subtest differed except Matrix Reasoning in RFAB DZ pairs, better in the twin who used (6.6, 0.6 to 12.7, P = 0.036); collapsing MZ and DZ left results non-significant. The MZ intervals include the between-family differences (−4.0, −3.4); the MTFS DZ interval excludes −3.4. Three printed P values do not match their intervals (by editors' calculation from the CI): Vocabulary MZ RFAB 0.098 (about 0.07 from the CI), Matrix Reasoning MZ 0.305 (about 0.12), Information DZ 0.545 (about 0.27).

anchors.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table S6
anchors.extracted: MTFS only, 47 pairs in which one twin never used and the other used more than 30 times and/or daily for a period: Vocabulary −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6, P = 0.481), Information 0.2, Block Design −1.6, Picture Arrangement 5.2; none significant.

anchors.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 3rd to 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Those missing cannabis data had lower SES and baseline IQ; in the RFAB 323 twins lacked follow-up IQ (466 tested at follow-up), handled by maximum likelihood under missing at random. Users heterogeneous (experimentation to regular use); recency and current against former use not measured; recall-based measures; all still young adults at last test, which the authors offer as a possible reason for the difference from Dunedin (tested at 38).

anchors.locator: Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences in IQ Be Attributed to a Possible Causal Effect of Marijuana Use?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion
anchors.extracted: The authors conclude that the decline reflects familial (mainly family-wide environmental) confounding rather than a neurotoxic effect, citing baseline differences, no dose-response and no co-twin difference. They also acknowledge modest numbers of discordant pairs and that they cannot rule out an effect of long-term use.

key_findings.note: Table 2 differences recomputed: Vocabulary 98.8 − 100.7 = −1.9, Block Design 98.7 − 100.7 = −2.0, Information 97.9 − 101.2 = −3.3 (text −2.7).
All values are in Table 3. Fig. 1, named in the locator, was not inspected (pane hidden).

The pooled-MZ-and-DZ sentence in the text comes before the Matrix Reasoning result and refers to the other five subtests. The note's point that the MZ intervals include the between-family differences is right; the MTFS DZ interval (−2.8 to 3.3, 99 pairs) excludes −3.4 (see missed).

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed from the intervals: about 0.07, 0.12 and 0.27 against the printed 0.098, 0.305 and 0.545. The other 13 Table 5 P values agree with their intervals to within about 0.02.
Checked against Meier et al. (2012) Table 2, which lists Picture Completion and no Picture Arrangement.

Partly checked: the year-of-age analysis's n of 785 and 2,271, against 789 and 2,277, is confirmed. The Fig. 1 half (e.g., the RFAB never-used start of about 99.4 against 100.2 in Table 2) was not checked, because the figure could not be viewed with the pane hidden. Targeted check needed for that half.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall, driven by RFAB missing data: 35% of eligible twins lacked cannabis data and 41% of those analysed had no follow-up IQ, with missingness linked to lower SES and IQ. The confounding domain (some concerns) is judged for the co-twin estimates, as the card says; the between-family estimates would be high.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and conclusion read imprecise, non-significant co-twin differences as showing that the association is not causal; 'completely eliminated' overstates −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6); and the baseline-difference argument holds in only one cohort.

missed: Balance for key finding 8 and the interpretation gap: in the largest discordant group, MTFS DZ pairs (99), the Vocabulary interval (0.2, −2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family difference of −3.4. The MZ intervals include it. So the co-twin evidence is not uniformly 'compatible with both'; it leans towards a smaller within-pair effect in the MTFS.

The phrase 'fell 3.4 to 4.0 points further behind age peers' (results_show, and the claim) is a difference in change between groups. On the raw Table 2 Vocabulary means, those who used fell 1.8 (RFAB) and 2.5 (MTFS) points, while those who did not rose 1.8 and 1.3. About half the gap is the comparison group's rise, which matters for readers who take it as a loss of 4 IQ points.
